How to Get Paid as a Freelancer: Invoices, Contracts, Deposits and Client Payments

Doing great work is half the job; getting paid for it is the other half. Follow Efe's made-up story through pricing structures, agreements, invoices, payment methods, international clients, late payers, scams and money systems, with scripts and a step-by-step setup plan.

By Princess Immanuel · Founder, Her Digital Playbook

Come sit with me, love, and bring a cup of something warm, because I want to tell you about a woman named Efe, and about the single most uncomfortable subject in all of freelancing: money.

Efe is twenty-nine, a freelance graphic designer who works from a tiny corner of her sister's flat, with a second-hand monitor and a mug that says "Draft 7." She is very, very good at her work. Clients tell her so. And yet, on a Tuesday evening in the middle of the month, she is sitting on the edge of her bed, staring at her phone, with a sinking feeling that has become horribly familiar. She finished a logo and brand pack six weeks ago. The client loved it. He said "thank you so much." And he has not paid.

She types a message. Deletes it. Types another. Deletes it. "I do not want to seem rude," she tells her sister Ese, who is folding laundry. "He might be having a hard time. What if he thinks I am pushy?" Ese, who works in a bank and has no patience for this kind of thing, says, "Efe. You did the work. He accepted the work. That is not pushy. That is Tuesday."

I want you to hear what Ese said, babe, because it might change something for you. Getting paid is not a favour you ask for. It is the normal, expected last step of doing a job. And yet so many talented women, designers, writers, assistants, editors, coaches, struggle with exactly this. Not because they are weak, but because nobody taught them how to set things up so that getting paid is automatic, clear and calm.

So that is what this guide is. It is a complete payment setup. We will follow Efe from that uncomfortable Tuesday to a calm, organized way of working where money arrives on time, most of the time, and when it does not, she knows exactly what to do. Efe is a made-up woman. She does not exist, and her numbers are examples, not results anyone should expect. But I have written her story with the ordinary moments of someone learning something hard, including a scam attempt that made her stomach drop.

By the end of this guide, you will understand the price structures that protect you, such as deposits, milestones and retainers. You will know what belongs in a simple agreement and how to write an invoice that gets paid. You will know the main ways of receiving money, their fees and risks, and how to get paid by clients in other countries. You will have a calm, step-by-step method for late payments, with scripts. You will know how to spot payment scams, how to organize your money and records, and how to have the awkward conversations without losing sleep. And you will finish with a thirty-day plan to set the whole system up.

Two honest notes. First, I am not a lawyer, accountant or tax adviser, and rules about contracts, taxes, payments and consumer rights differ widely by country, so please treat this guide as a map and check the details for your own situation. Second, no system can guarantee that every client pays, but a good one makes non-payment rare, and gives you a clear path when it happens.

Ready? Let's go back to a bedroom, a half-folded pile of laundry and a very long message that Efe cannot bring herself to send.

1The Painful Truth: Getting Paid Is A Skill

Efe finally sends a short message. "Hi Mr. Okoye, I hope you are well. Just checking in on the invoice for the brand pack." Mr. Okoye replies, forty minutes later, "Oh, I forgot! I will send it this week." She exhales. A week passes. Then another. She feels foolish and anxious in equal parts.

Let me tell you what Efe worked out over the next few weeks, love, because it is the key to this entire guide. Almost every payment problem is really a setup problem. The client was not necessarily a villain. Efe had simply built a way of working where there was no deposit, no clear due date, no written agreement and an invoice that she sent weeks late. Almost anyone would have slipped under those conditions.

Why freelancers struggle to get paid

  • Vague agreements. "I'll design your logo" without defining what is included, when payment is due or what happens if things change.
  • No deposit. Doing all the work first, then asking for all the money, leaves you with no protection.
  • Late or messy invoices. An invoice sent a month after delivery, with no due date, almost guarantees delay.
  • Awkwardness about money. Many women feel guilty asking, and clients can sense it.
  • No follow-up system. Without reminders, unpaid invoices drift.
  • Unclear scope. "Just one more small change" becomes ten hours of free work.
  • Working with the wrong clients. Some people will never pay on time, however clear you are.
  • No safety buffer. If a payment is late and you have no savings, panic sets in.

The good news

Each one of those has a fix. And the fixes are boring, simple and repeatable: a deposit, a short agreement, a clear invoice, a polite reminder sequence and a small financial cushion. When you set them up once, you reuse them for every client.

The mindset shift

Think of payment terms the way a restaurant thinks of its menu. A restaurant does not apologize for charging for the meal, and it does not feel awkward about the bill arriving at the end. The price and the process are simply part of the experience. You can run your work the same way: clear, calm and expected.

What good payment looks like

A healthy payment setup means:

  • Clients know the price and the terms before work begins.
  • You are paid something upfront, so you are never working entirely on trust.
  • Invoices are clear, prompt and easy to pay.
  • Late payments follow a simple, polite process you do not have to invent each time.
  • You have a buffer, so one late payment is an annoyance, not a crisis.

Efe's lesson

Efe writes on a sticky note: "Payment is part of the job, not a favour." She sticks it above her monitor, next to "Draft 7." Ese, passing with a basket of laundry, reads it and says, "That should be on a poster." Efe says, "It is going on a poster."

2Price Structures That Protect You

A few weeks after Mr. Okoye finally pays, a new client contacts Efe: a small restaurant wants a full brand identity. She feels the familiar flutter of excitement and then, immediately, the familiar flutter of fear. "How do I price this so it does not happen again?" she asks Ese over dinner. Ese says, "Get money before you start. Always. It is not complicated."

Ese is right, babe, but let me explain how to do it without feeling awkward, because the way you structure a price is your first and strongest protection.

The four main structures

StructureWhat it isBest forProtects you by
Fixed price with a depositOne price for a defined project, part paid upfrontProjects with clear deliverablesSecuring commitment before you start
Milestone paymentsThe price split into stages, each paid on completionLarger or longer projectsSpreading risk, so you are never far ahead of payment
Hourly rateYou charge for time workedUnclear scopes or ongoing supportPaying you for every hour, but needs honest tracking
RetainerA fixed monthly fee for ongoing supportRegular, repeat workGiving predictable income, paid at the start of each month

The deposit: your strongest protection

A deposit is part of the price paid before you begin. It does three things: it confirms the client is serious, it covers your time if they disappear, and it makes the rest of the payment far more likely. Many freelancers ask for around half upfront on smaller projects, and use milestones on larger ones. Your own policy can differ, but have one.

How to say it, simply and without apology:

The project fee is $600. I start work once the 50 percent deposit of $300 is received, and the balance is due on delivery of the final files.

Milestones for bigger projects

Split the price into logical stages tied to deliverables. For example, a brand identity might look like this:

StageWhat is deliveredPayment
StartAgreement signed, project begins40 percent
ConceptsThree logo concepts presented30 percent
Final filesFinal logo and brand pack delivered30 percent

You do not release the next stage's work until the previous payment is made. This keeps you from being far ahead of what you have been paid.

Hourly pricing, carefully

Hourly rates suit work where the scope is unclear or ongoing. To protect yourself, agree an estimate or a cap in advance, track your hours honestly and send itemized invoices. Be aware that clients may worry about the total, so be transparent.

Retainers

A retainer is a monthly fee for a set amount of support. Invoice it at the start of the month, not the end. State what is included, how extra work is charged and the notice period for ending it. Retainers make income steadier, which is wonderful for your peace of mind.

Minimum fees and kill fees

  • A minimum project fee prevents you from taking on tiny jobs that cost more in time than they earn.
  • A kill fee is a payment due if the client cancels after work has begun, covering the time you already spent. State it in your agreement.

Include costs in your price

If you pay for tools, stock images, fonts or platform fees to deliver a project, include those in your price, or list them separately. Do not absorb costs you did not plan for.

Pricing so that fees do not eat you

Payment platforms and bank transfers often charge fees, and international transfers may involve exchange rates. Work out what you will actually receive, and price accordingly. Never calculate your price only from the number on the invoice.

Efe's new structure

Efe drafts a new pricing sheet with three tiers and a clear structure: 50 percent upfront, 50 percent on delivery for projects under $500, and three milestones for anything larger. She tells the restaurant owner, calmly, "I start once the deposit is received." There is a small pause, and the owner says, "That is fine. Send me the invoice." Efe releases a breath she did not know she had been holding. She writes on her sticky note: "Deposit first. Always."

3The Agreement: Scope, Revisions And Payment Terms

A week later, the restaurant owner pays the deposit, and Efe begins the work. Two weeks in, the owner emails: "Could you also design the menu? And the signage? And maybe business cards? You are so talented." Efe's stomach tightens. She had agreed to a logo and a brand pack. She stares at the email, chewing her pen, and thinks: "If I say no, will she be upset? If I say yes, I will work for free."

Let me tell you what Efe learned from this, love, and what protected her. A short written agreement is not about distrust. It is about making sure both people picture the same thing. It is the difference between a smooth project and a quietly resentful one.

What to put in a simple agreement

You do not need a ten-page legal document for a small project, but you do need things in writing. Cover these points:

ItemWhat it should say
The partiesWho you are and who the client is
The scopeExactly what you will deliver, in plain words
What is not includedAnything outside the scope
The timelineKey dates and deadlines, and what you need from the client by when
RevisionsHow many rounds of changes are included, and the price of extra ones
The price and payment scheduleThe total, the deposit, the milestones, due dates and accepted payment methods
Late paymentWhat happens if an invoice is not paid on time
Cancellation and kill feeWhat happens if either side ends the project early
Ownership of the workWhen rights transfer to the client, usually after full payment
ConfidentialityWhat each side keeps private
CreditWhether you may show the work in your portfolio

A friendly sample

Here is an example you can adapt. It is not legal advice, and you should check the rules where you live and consider professional advice for larger projects.

Project Agreement > > Between: [Your name] and [Client name] > > What I will deliver: A logo (three initial concepts, one chosen and refined) and a basic brand pack (colours, fonts and usage guide). Final files in common formats. > > Not included: Menus, signage, printed materials and business cards. These can be quoted separately. > > Timeline: First concepts within 7 working days of receiving the brief and deposit. Final files within 10 working days of approval. > > Revisions: Two rounds of changes are included. Further changes are $40 per hour. > > Fee: $600. A deposit of $300 is due before I begin, and the balance is due within 7 days of delivery of the final files. I accept [payment methods]. > > Late payment: Invoices unpaid after the due date may pause further work and incur a late fee of [amount or percentage], as agreed here. > > Cancellation: If the project is cancelled after work has begun, I will invoice for work completed up to that point, and the deposit is non-refundable. > > Ownership: Rights to the final files transfer to the client once the full fee is paid. I may show the work in my portfolio unless you tell me otherwise. > > Confidentiality: Both of us will keep private information confidential. > > Agreed by: ________________ Date: ________

How to get it signed

A simple reply like "Yes, I agree" by email can serve as acceptance, and many platforms offer simple electronic signature tools. For larger projects, use a signed document, and keep copies.

Scope creep and the polite "no"

Scope creep is when a project quietly grows beyond what was agreed. Your agreement gives you a calm, professional answer. For Efe's restaurant owner:

Thank you so much for your kind words. The menu, signage and business cards are outside our current agreement, but I'd love to help. I can send you a separate quote for those. Would you like me to do that?

Notice there is no apology and no drama. You are not refusing. You are offering a paid next step.

Revisions

Define how many rounds are included. Without a limit, "just one more tweak" can go on forever. When the included revisions are used, politely quote for more.

Ownership and portfolio

Decide when the client owns the final work, usually after full payment, and whether you may show it in your portfolio. Both are normal things to agree upfront.

Efe's response

Efe sends the polite reply, and the restaurant owner answers, "Oh, of course, yes please quote me for the menu." Efe sends a new quote the next day, with a new deposit. The scope creep turns into a second paid project. She writes on her sticky note: "Scope in writing. Extras get quotes." She sends a photo of the wall of notes to Ese, who replies with a row of applause emojis.

4Invoices That Actually Get Paid

On a Friday evening, Efe finishes the restaurant's brand pack and feels a glow of satisfaction. She zips the files, writes a warm message and then realizes she has not made the invoice. She opens a blank document, types "Invoice," stares at it and thinks, "I have no idea what this is supposed to say." She texts Ese: "What goes on an invoice?" Ese replies in thirty seconds with a bullet list and a photo of the invoice template her bank uses. "Copy the structure," she writes. "Not the logo."

Let me give you that list, babe, because an invoice is a small document with a big job: it turns "I did the work" into "please pay me this, by this date, in this way." A clear invoice is far more likely to be paid on time than a vague message.

What every invoice should include

ItemWhy it matters
The word "Invoice" and an invoice numberMakes it easy to track and refer to
Your name or business name and contact detailsSo they know who to pay and how to reach you
Client's name and detailsShows who it is addressed to
Invoice date and due dateThe due date is the most important line
A clear description of the workMatches the agreement, with no mystery
Quantities, rates and the totalItemize where helpful
Deposits already paid and the balance dueAvoids confusion
Payment methods and detailsMake it easy to pay, with exact instructions
Payment terms and late fee, if anyMatches your agreement
A short thank-you noteA human touch

Make it easy to pay

The easiest invoice to pay is one where the client does not have to ask a question. Include the exact account details or payment link, the currency and the reference to use. If you offer more than one method, list them clearly.

Send it promptly

Send the invoice the moment the work is delivered, or on the day the milestone is reached, not a week later. The faster the invoice arrives, the fresher the client's goodwill, and the sooner the payment clock starts.

Choose a due date and stick to it

"Due on receipt," "due in seven days" and "due in fourteen days" are all common choices. Shorter terms are better for small projects. Whatever you choose, state it clearly. A vague "please pay soon" is an invitation to forget.

Number your invoices

Use a simple sequence, such as 001, 002, 003 or a date-based system. It makes your records tidy and helps clients' accounts teams.

Use simple tools

You can make a clear invoice with a document or spreadsheet template, or use an invoicing tool or the invoicing feature in a payment service. Choose whatever you will actually use consistently. Many tools can send reminders automatically and let clients pay online.

A sample invoice

INVOICE 004 > > From: Efe [Surname], [email], [phone] > To: [Client name], [business], [email] > Invoice date: 12 March Due date: 19 March > > | Description | Amount | > |---|---| > | Brand identity project: logo and brand pack | $600.00 | > | Less deposit paid on 22 February | -$300.00 | > | Balance due | $300.00 | > > Payment details: [bank details or payment link], please use "Invoice 004" as the reference. > Terms: Payment due within 7 days. Late payments may incur a fee as agreed in our project agreement. > > Thank you so much for working with me!

Keep a record

Save every invoice in a folder, organized by month, and track which are paid, unpaid or overdue in a simple sheet. We will build that system later.

Efe's first clean invoice

Efe builds her first proper invoice in a spreadsheet, copies the structure from Ese's bank template and adds a friendly thank-you line. She sends it within an hour of delivering the files, with the due date in bold. The restaurant owner pays in three days, with a message that says, "That was so easy!" Efe stares at the notification. "It was easy because I made it easy," she says aloud. Ese, in the kitchen, says, "Finally she understands."

5The Payment Methods Map

A few days later, Efe has a new problem, and a pleasant one: two different clients want to pay her, and they have suggested different methods. One wants to send a bank transfer. The other asks, "Can I pay you through an app?" Efe opens her mouth, closes it and says, "Let me get back to you."

Let me lay out the map for you, love, because choosing how to be paid affects your fees, your protection and how quickly the money lands. Methods differ by country and change over time, so please check what is available and allowed where you live.

The main ways to receive money

MethodHow it worksTypical strengthsTypical drawbacks
Bank transferMoney goes directly from the client's bank to yoursOften low cost within a country; clear recordsCan be slow or costly across borders; limited buyer protection
Payment apps and walletsA service holds and moves money between accountsFast, easy for clients; often a record of the transactionFees; limits; account holds or restrictions can occur
Online payment links and card paymentsThe client pays by card through a linkConvenient for clients; professionalProcessing fees; chargebacks are possible
Marketplace or platform paymentsA freelance platform holds payment and releases it on completionEscrow-style protection for both sidesPlatform fees; platform rules; withdrawal times
International payment servicesServices designed to receive money in other currenciesOften better rates and local-style account detailsFees; availability depends on country; verification required
ChequesPaper paymentFamiliar in some placesSlow; can bounce; used in overpayment scams
CashPhysical moneyImmediateNo record; safety and tax concerns
Digital currenciesPayments in crypto assetsSometimes allowed across bordersVolatile value; rules vary widely and some places restrict them; scams are common. Treat with great care

How to choose

Ask these questions about any method:

  • What does it cost me, including fees, exchange rates and withdrawal costs?
  • How fast does the money become usable, in my bank or in cash?
  • What protection do I have if there is a dispute, a mistake or a scam?
  • Is it allowed and reliable in my country?
  • Is it easy for my client? If it is awkward, they will pay late.
  • Does it give me a clear record for taxes and bookkeeping?

Offer one or two, not ten

Too many options confuse people and create admin. Choose one primary method and one backup, and put the details on every invoice.

Protect your accounts

Use strong, unique passwords and two-step verification on every payment account. Never share your login. Beware of emails that pretend to be from a payment service and ask you to "verify" your account by clicking a link, which is a common trick.

Check the terms

Read the terms of each service about holds, limits, disputes and closures, so you are not surprised. Keep a small amount in more than one place if you can, so a hold on one account does not freeze everything.

Where to go to learn what works in your country

Look at your bank's website for how to receive international payments, search for guidance from freelancer communities in your own country and read official consumer or financial authority websites about payment services. Ask experienced freelancers what they use, and why. Always verify any advice yourself.

Efe chooses

Efe talks to three other freelancers in a local designers' group, reads her bank's guidance and chooses a bank transfer as her main method for local clients and an international payment service for overseas clients. She puts both on her invoice template. "Two options," she tells Ese. "Not twelve." Ese says, "A miracle."

6Getting Paid From Abroad

It is a warm afternoon in June, and Efe receives an email from a client in another country, a small design studio. "We love your portfolio," it says. "Can you design our new website graphics? We can pay in dollars." Efe's heart does a flip. She forwards it to Ese, who reads it slowly and says, "Be careful. International money has layers."

Let me walk you through the layers, babe, because getting paid from other countries can be a wonderful opportunity and a source of surprises.

The layers of international payment

LayerWhat to think about
CurrencyIn what currency will they pay? Exchange rates move, and conversion has a cost
FeesThe sender's service, intermediary banks and your own bank may each take a fee
SpeedSome transfers take days
RulesSome countries have limits, reporting rules or restrictions on certain payments
VerificationServices may ask for identity documents before you can receive money
TaxesIncome from abroad is usually still income for tax purposes where you live
Time zonesSlow replies can delay payments

Price in a way that protects you

  • Choose the invoice currency deliberately. Invoicing in a more stable, widely used currency can protect you from sudden changes, but check what is practical for your client and your bank.
  • Add the fees to your thinking. Work out what will actually land in your account.
  • Consider a small buffer for exchange-rate movement on longer projects.
  • State who pays the transfer fees in your agreement. Many freelancers ask clients to cover their own sending fees so the full amount arrives.

Check before you commit

Before you agree to a project, find out:

  • Which payment methods are available between your country and theirs.
  • What the total cost and delay will be.
  • Whether there are any rules about receiving this kind of payment where you live.
  • How you will withdraw the money in local currency.

If there is a restriction you cannot work around, be honest with the client early, and find another solution.

Use clear, professional documentation

International clients often appreciate a clear invoice in their currency, the exact amount, bank or service details, a reference and a due date. Include your full name as it appears on your account, so the payment is matched correctly.

Taxes on foreign income

In most places, income from foreign clients still counts as income. Rules may include declaring it, paying tax and sometimes handling forms or registrations. Some clients, especially in certain countries, may ask for tax forms, such as those confirming your tax residency. I am not a tax adviser, so check what applies to you and consider professional advice. Keep records of every payment, conversion and fee.

Be careful about who you work for

Some international "clients" are scammers who prey on freelancers. Verify who they are, check their business, ask for a written agreement and take a deposit through a trusted method. We will cover scam patterns shortly.

Efe's first international payment

Efe asks the studio for a 50 percent deposit and states in her agreement that they will cover sending fees. She uses an international payment service she researched, set up with identity checks, and sends the invoice in dollars. The deposit arrives in four days, with a small fee deducted. She notes the exact amount in her sheet, converts it and writes the figure on a sticky note. "This is what actually lands," she says. "Not what the invoice says." Ese nods. "Always know what actually lands."

7Late Payment: The Calm Sequence

It is the first week of July, and Efe has a problem. An invoice for $450, due ten days ago, is unpaid. The client, a small online shop, had been friendly and quick during the project. Now there is silence. Efe feels her old, familiar dread, a hot knot in her stomach, and her hand hovers over her phone.

Ese, passing with a mug of tea, says, "Do the sequence."

Efe says, "What sequence?"

Ese grins. "The one you are about to write."

This is the part that frightens most freelancers, love, so let me give you a simple, repeatable sequence you can follow without drama. The goal is to be polite, clear and consistent, and to treat late payment as a business matter, not a personal one.

First, remember what is probably happening

In most cases, late payment is not malicious. The client forgot, their finances are tight, the invoice went to the wrong person or an approval is stuck. A calm reminder usually solves it. A small number of clients delay on purpose, which is why you also need a firm path.

The reminder timeline

WhenWhat to do
A few days before the due dateSend a friendly heads-up that the invoice is coming due
The day after the due dateSend a short, polite reminder with the invoice attached again
Seven days afterSend a firmer message referencing the agreement and any late fee
Fourteen days afterPause any further work, send a formal reminder and offer a payment plan if appropriate
Thirty days afterSend a final notice, consider next steps and decide how much more effort the invoice is worth

Scripts you can adapt

Before the due date:

Hi [Name], just a quick note that invoice 004 is due on [date]. Please let me know if you need anything from me. Thank you!

The day after:

Hi [Name], I hope you are well. I wanted to check in on invoice 004, which was due yesterday. I have attached it again for convenience. Please let me know if you need any details.

One week after:

Hi [Name], I'm following up on invoice 004 for $450, which was due on [date] and is now seven days overdue. As per our agreement, payment was due within seven days of delivery. Could you let me know when I can expect payment? If there's an issue, I'm happy to talk it through.

Two weeks after, firmer:

Hi [Name], invoice 004 is now fourteen days overdue. Under our agreement, a late fee of [amount] now applies, and I'm pausing further work until the invoice is paid. I'd like to resolve this quickly. Please confirm today when payment will be made, or let me know if you'd like to discuss a payment plan.

A final notice:

Hi [Name], this is my final reminder for invoice 004, which is now thirty days overdue. If I do not receive payment or a clear plan by [date], I will have to consider further steps, which may include a formal demand or other action permitted where I live. I'd much prefer to settle this directly, so please get in touch.

Keep the tone calm and factual

Do not insult, threaten or lose your temper. Stick to the facts: the work was delivered, the invoice was sent, the due date has passed. A calm, consistent tone protects your reputation and your peace.

Use a different channel

If emails go unanswered, try a message on another platform, or a short phone call, which can be harder to ignore. Document everything.

Pause the work

If your agreement allows, stop further work and withhold final files until payment. This is why releasing files after full payment, or in stages, is wise.

Offer a payment plan

Sometimes a client genuinely cannot pay in one go. A short written payment plan, with dates and amounts, can be better than nothing. Put it in writing.

Further options

If a client still does not pay, options may include a formal demand letter, a collections service, mediation, a small claims or similar process or professional legal advice. The right path depends on your country, the amount and your agreement, and costs and time can outweigh the amount owed on small invoices. I cannot give legal advice, so check what applies to you and decide how much effort an unpaid invoice is worth.

Learn from it

When an invoice goes badly late, ask: Did I take a deposit? Was the agreement clear? Did I vet the client? Did I invoice promptly? Use each case to improve your setup.

Efe sends the sequence

Efe follows the timeline. The day after the due date, she sends a polite note. A week later, she sends the firmer one. On day fourteen, the client finally replies: "So sorry, we had a banking issue! Paying today." The money arrives that evening. Efe stares at it, laughs and says to Ese, "I did not cry once." Ese says, "Growth." Efe adds the sequence scripts to a folder called "Reminders," and for the first time, a late invoice does not ruin her week.

8Payment Scams: The Ones That Catch Freelancers

On a Wednesday morning, Efe receives a lovely email. A stranger, apparently the head of a small company abroad, writes: "We love your work and would like to hire you for a large poster campaign. Our budget is $2,500. We will send payment immediately." Efe's hands go cold with excitement. She replies, and within an hour, a payment notification arrives: $4,000. The sender writes: "Oh no, my assistant sent too much! Please send back the extra $1,500 to my 'courier' and keep the rest as a bonus for your trouble."

Efe's stomach drops, not with joy this time, but with a prickle of something wrong. She stares at the numbers, then calls Ese. Ese says one word: "Overpayment." Then another: "Scam."

Efe is lucky, babe, because she had a sister who knew. Let me teach you the patterns, because these tricks cost freelancers real money every day, and I want you protected.

The overpayment scam

A "client" sends you more than you agreed, often by a method that later reverses, such as a fake cheque or a payment that is later cancelled, and asks you to send the difference to someone else. By the time the original payment is revealed to be fake or reversed, you have sent real money and are left owing it to your bank.

What to do: Never send money back from an overpayment unless you have confirmed, with your bank, that the original payment has fully cleared and cannot be reversed. In most cases, simply refuse, and ask the sender to reverse their own payment.

Fake payment screenshots

A "client" sends a screenshot showing that payment has been made, and asks you to deliver. The money never arrives.

What to do: Never rely on a screenshot. Check your own account for the actual funds.

The "pay for software" or "pay for a background check" trick

Someone offers a job, then asks you to pay for software, training, equipment or a check before you begin.

What to do: Real clients do not ask you to pay to work for them. Walk away.

Fake invoices and payment-detail changes

Scammers pretend to be a supplier, a client or a payment service and send an email saying "our bank details have changed," or they send a fake invoice that looks real.

What to do: Verify any change of payment details by contacting the person through a separate, trusted channel. Do not click links in unexpected emails, and go directly to the official website of any service.

Phishing for your payment account

You receive an email claiming your payment account is "locked" or "at risk," with a link to "verify" your details.

What to do: Do not click. Go to the service directly, and use two-step verification.

Chargebacks and disputes

Even legitimate clients can sometimes dispute a card payment or request a reversal, and some bad actors use disputes to get work for free. This is more likely with card and some app payments.

What to do: Keep a record of your agreement, communications and delivered work. Understand each payment service's dispute process, and deliver final files only after payment has fully cleared, where possible.

Red flags

Red flagWhat it often means
A very large budget for a vague projectA scam hoping you will not ask questions
Overpayment and a request for a refund to another personThe overpayment scam
Pressure to hurryThey do not want you to think
A "client" who refuses a call, a contract or a deposit through a trusted methodPossible fraud
Requests for passwords or banking loginsAccount theft
Poor English from a supposedly large company, a free email address or a brand-new profilePossible fake identity
Payment before any conversationOften the overpayment trick

Protect yourself

  • Vet new clients: search the name and company, check their website and social presence and ask for a call.
  • Use written agreements and deposits through trusted methods.
  • Check your actual balance before delivering final files.
  • Never send money to receive money.
  • Keep your accounts secure, with strong, unique passwords and two-step verification.
  • Trust your gut. If something feels off, pause and ask someone you trust.
Common Mistake 🚨 Never pay to get work, never send back part of an overpayment before your bank confirms the funds are final, and never share passwords or banking logins.

Efe's response

Efe replies to the "client": "Thank you, but I am not able to refund an overpayment. Please reverse the transaction through your own bank." The scammer replies with three increasingly aggressive messages and then vanishes. Efe contacts her bank, which confirms the payment was suspicious and reversed it within days. She reports the sender to the platform. "I almost sent them my money," she tells Ese, shaken. Ese hugs her. "But you did not."

She writes on her wall of sticky notes: "No refunds on overpayments. Ever." And underneath, in smaller letters: "Call Ese."

9Build A Simple Money System

By autumn, Efe's income has become... lumpy. Some months, three clients pay at once, and she feels rich. Other months, nothing arrives until the twentieth, and she watches her rent date like a hawk. She says to Ese, in a small voice, "I am earning enough overall. Why does it feel so frightening?"

Ese, who has watched many clients with irregular incomes at the bank, says, "Because you do not have a system. Freelance money needs pots."

She is right, love, and I want to teach you what she meant. The problem with freelance income is not only getting paid. It is managing money that arrives unevenly. A simple system turns lumpy income into steady life.

Separate your money

If you can, open a separate account or pot for your business income, so you can see what is yours and what is for taxes and costs. Mixing everything together makes it impossible to know where you stand.

The money pots

When a payment arrives, divide it straight away into pots. Here is an example, with illustrative shares that will differ for you.

PotWhat it is forExample share
Tax and obligationsMoney you must not touch20 to 30 percent, depending on your rules
Business costsTools, software, fees and courses5 to 10 percent
BufferA cushion for slow months and late payments10 percent until it reaches two to three months of costs
YouYour payThe rest

Decide your shares in advance, so you never accidentally spend your tax money.

Pay yourself a "salary"

Instead of spending whatever happens to be in the account, move a regular amount from your business pot to your personal account each month, like a wage. In good months, extra stays in the buffer. In slow months, the buffer pays the wage. This single habit makes freelance life feel calm.

Build a buffer

A buffer of one to three months of essential costs turns a late payment into an inconvenience. Build it slowly from every payment until it is full, and then keep it for emergencies.

Forecast gently

Once a month, write down what you expect to receive and what you need to pay over the next two or three months. You do not need to be precise. A rough forecast shows you when a slow stretch is coming, so you can prepare.

Keep simple books

Keep a spreadsheet with: date, client, invoice number, amount, date paid, method, fees and notes. Record every expense and receipt. This takes ten minutes a week and makes taxes calmer.

DateClientInvoiceAmountDuePaidFeesNotes

Track your true income

Look at your monthly profit: income minus costs and fees. And look at your hourly rate, the profit divided by all the hours you worked, including admin and finding clients. If it is lower than you expected, your prices or scope need work.

Review monthly

Once a month, answer four questions: How much came in? How much is overdue? What did I spend? What is one change for next month? A monthly money check keeps small problems from growing.

Efe's pots

Efe opens a separate account and sets up three pots: tax, costs and buffer. She decides to pay herself a fixed amount on the first of each month. The first month feels strange, because it seems like she is "losing" money from each payment. By month three, a client pays twelve days late, and Efe's life does not wobble at all. She texts Ese: "I have a buffer." Ese replies: "You have a business." Efe puts her phone down and looks at the ceiling for a while, smiling.

10Taxes And Records: Be Curious, Not Scared

On a Sunday afternoon, Efe's cousin Tobi, who lives abroad, calls for a chat and says casually, "Do you pay tax on your freelance money?" Efe goes quiet. She has been telling herself she will "look into it later." She says, "I... am working on it." Tobi laughs kindly. "Everyone says that. Do it this month."

Let me give you the gentle version, babe, because tax fear is real, and avoiding it makes it worse. I am not a tax adviser or accountant, and rules differ enormously, so treat this as a map.

What to find out

  • Do I need to register as self-employed or as a business where I live?
  • How is my freelance income taxed, and are there thresholds or special rules?
  • When are payments and filings due?
  • What can I deduct as business costs?
  • Do I need to charge or report any sales taxes or VAT on services?
  • How are foreign payments treated, and are there any forms I need?
  • Are there social contributions, pensions or insurance I should plan for?

Where to go for answers

Start with your government's official website for self-employed people or small businesses, which usually has plain-language guidance. Local freelancer communities can share experience, but always verify with official sources. For anything complicated, a qualified accountant or tax adviser often pays for themselves.

Practical habits

  • Set aside a share of every payment the day it arrives.
  • Keep every invoice, receipt and bank record, organized by month.
  • Record foreign payments with the amount received, the date and the conversion.
  • Separate business and personal spending where you can.
  • Put tax dates in your calendar.
  • Do not ignore letters or notices. Respond promptly.

Why records matter beyond tax

Good records help you prove your income when applying for loans, rent or visas, resolve disputes and see how your business is really doing.

Efe's afternoon

Efe spends an afternoon reading her government's guidance for freelancers and writing down three questions. She books a short appointment with an accountant, who explains her obligations in plain language and helps her set a sensible tax pot percentage. It costs a small amount and removes months of dread. "I wish I had done this a year ago," she says to Tobi on a video call. Tobi says, "Everyone does."

11The Awkward Conversations (And What To Say)

It is mid-November, and Efe has a list of conversations she has been avoiding: raising her prices, asking a client for a deposit, saying no to extra work, answering a refund request and chasing a client who has vanished. She writes them on a card, labelled "The Scary List," and pins it above her desk. Ese reads it and says, "You are going to cross all of these out."

"By when?"

"By Christmas."

She is right, love, and these conversations are not as terrible as they feel. The words matter, so here are the scripts Efe used. Adapt them to your own voice.

Asking for a deposit

Before I begin, I take a 50 percent deposit to secure your place in my schedule. Here is the invoice for the deposit. Once it's received, I'll start straight away.

When a client pushes back on the deposit

I understand. The deposit is how I reserve time and cover my costs, so I can give your project my full attention. It's part of how I work with every client. If that's a concern, I'm happy to split the payment into three stages instead.

Raising your prices for new clients

From [date], my rates for new projects will be [new rates]. I'm happy to give you the current rate for anything booked before then.

Raising prices for existing clients

Hi [Name], I wanted to let you know that from [date], my monthly rate will move from $200 to $230. I've loved working with you, and I'll keep delivering the same quality. If you'd like to lock in the current rate for the next three months, just let me know by [date].

Saying no to extra work

Thank you so much for thinking of me. That's outside our current agreement, but I'd be happy to quote for it separately. Would you like me to send a quote?

Responding to a request for a discount

I appreciate you asking. My prices reflect the work involved, so I can't reduce the fee, but I can offer a smaller version of the project for [price]. Would that suit you better?

Responding to a refund request

I'm sorry it wasn't what you hoped for. Could you tell me more about what's not working? I'd like to understand and see whether I can put it right. If we can't resolve it, I'll review your request in line with our agreement.

Always look at your agreement first, stay calm and be fair. A reasonable resolution, such as a partial fix or refund, can be cheaper than a dispute.

A client who has vanished

Hi [Name], I haven't heard from you since [date], and I want to make sure everything is okay. I'm keen to complete the project, but I need [specific thing] to continue. If I don't hear from you by [date], I'll pause the project and hold the work in progress until we can talk. Thank you!

Ending a working relationship

Thank you for the opportunity to work together. I've decided to focus on other projects, so I won't be able to continue after [date]. I'm happy to finish the current work and hand over everything neatly.

A few principles

  • Stay kind, clear and calm.
  • Do not over-explain or apologize.
  • Offer a next step, not only a refusal.
  • Put it in writing.
  • Practice out loud until the words stop feeling strange.

Efe crosses them out

Efe works through her Scary List over six weeks. The deposit conversation takes one minute. The price increase for new clients takes two. Saying no to extra work turns into a paid project. The discount request resolves with a smaller package. The vanished client reappears after her message, apologetic. By Christmas, the card is covered in crossed-out lines, and Efe takes a photo and sends it to Ese with the caption, "Done." Ese replies: "Told you."

12Retainers And Recurring Billing

In January, one of Efe's happiest clients, the restaurant owner, says: "Could you do our social graphics every month? I would love not to think about it." Efe's heart leaps. A repeat client! Then her stomach flutters. "How do I charge for something ongoing?" she asks Ese. Ese says, "At the start of the month. Always."

Let me give you the full picture, babe, because retainers can transform a freelance income from a roller coaster into something steadier, but only if they are set up well.

What a retainer is

A retainer is a regular, usually monthly, fee for an agreed amount of ongoing work or availability. Instead of selling each project separately, you sell a relationship.

Why they help you

  • Predictable income, which makes planning and budgeting possible.
  • Less time finding clients, because you keep the ones you have.
  • Deeper work, because you understand the client over time.
  • A simpler money process: one invoice a month, at the start.

What a good retainer agreement covers

ItemExample
What is included each month"Eight social graphics and two story templates"
Rhythm"Delivered in two batches, on the 8th and the 22nd"
Response time"I reply within two working days"
The monthly fee and due date"$320, invoiced on the 1st, due by the 5th"
Extras"Additional work at $35 per hour, quoted first"
Unused work"Unused deliverables do not roll over"
Notice to end or change"Thirty days' notice by either side"
Pausing work for non-payment"Work is paused if the invoice is unpaid after seven days"

Invoice at the start of the month

Billing in advance means you are paid before you work, which removes most late-payment risk and keeps your income steady. Say it plainly: "The monthly fee is invoiced on the first and due by the fifth."

Automate where you can

Many invoicing tools can send recurring invoices and reminders automatically. Check that the tool and the payment method suit you and your clients.

Price retainers fairly

A retainer should not simply be your hourly rate multiplied by hours. Consider the value, your costs and the stability you are offering. Review your price every few months, and raise it with notice as your results grow.

Protect your capacity

Do not take more retainers than you can serve well. A burned-out freelancer delivers worse work and loses clients. Keep a waiting list if you are full.

Efe's retainer

Efe offers the restaurant a "Monthly Social Pack" for a fixed fee, invoiced on the first of each month, with a clear scope, a thirty-day notice period and a rate for extras. The owner says yes. On the first day of the next month, she sends the invoice. It is paid in two days. Efe says to Ese, "It feels like a salary." Ese says, "That is the point."

13Slow-Paying Big Clients And Agencies

In spring, Efe lands a project with a large company, through an agency. The contract looks professional, the budget is generous and the agency's manager is charming. Then she reads the payment terms: "Payment within 60 days of invoice approval." Efe stares at the page. Sixty days. Ninety, if approval is slow. She calls Ese. "Is this normal?" Ese says, "Sadly, yes."

Let me explain, love, because larger organizations often work differently, and understanding it protects you from nasty surprises.

How larger clients usually pay

  • Longer payment terms, such as thirty, forty-five or sixty days from the invoice date or from approval.
  • Approval processes, where your invoice must be approved by one person, then another, before payment is released.
  • Vendor registration, where you may need to complete forms, provide tax details or be added to a supplier list.
  • Invoice portals, where you upload invoices through a specific system.
  • Set payment runs, such as paying on certain days of the month.

Protect yourself

  • Ask about payment terms before you agree, not after the work.
  • Negotiate where you can: shorter terms, a deposit or milestone payments, particularly for larger projects.
  • Build the delay into your cash flow. Do not plan to pay rent from an invoice that will arrive in sixty days.
  • Ask exactly how invoicing works: who receives it, what format, what approvals and what dates.
  • Submit invoices correctly and promptly, with every required detail, such as purchase order numbers.
  • Follow up politely and consistently, because invoices in large systems can sit in someone's inbox.

Questions to ask a larger client

  • What are your standard payment terms?
  • Who should the invoice be addressed to, and is there a purchase order number?
  • Do you have a preferred invoicing system or format?
  • How long does approval usually take?
  • How do you pay: by bank transfer, platform or another method?
  • Do I need to complete any supplier or tax forms?

Agencies and middlemen

If you work through an agency or a platform, check whether they pay you only after their client pays them, since that can delay your money further. Read the terms carefully, and ask for clear commitments about when you will be paid.

Efe negotiates

Efe emails the agency: "Thank you for the contract. Could we agree a 30 percent deposit upfront and thirty-day terms on the balance? That helps me plan for a project of this size." The manager replies, "That should be fine, let me check." A day later: "Approved." Efe whoops quietly, then looks around for Ese, who is not there. She tells the sofa instead.

14Platforms, Marketplaces And Escrow

During the summer, Efe tries a freelance marketplace for the first time, hoping to find new clients. She loves the way the platform holds the client's payment until she delivers, but she is surprised by the fees, and by how long her withdrawal takes. "I have been paid," she tells Ese, "but the money is somewhere in a pipe."

Let me explain how these work, babe, because platforms can be a wonderful way to find clients and a source of payment surprises.

How platform payments usually work

  • The client funds the project, and the platform holds the money, often called escrow.
  • You deliver the work, and the client approves it, or approval happens automatically after a period.
  • The platform releases the money to your account balance.
  • You withdraw to your bank or payment service, sometimes after a waiting period.

The advantages

  • Protection for both sides. The client knows the money is committed, and you know it exists.
  • A record. Everything is tracked.
  • Dispute processes. If there is a disagreement, the platform can mediate.

The things to watch

ItemWhy it matters
FeesPlatforms usually take a percentage, and there may be withdrawal and currency conversion fees
Hold timesFunds may be held for days after approval
Withdrawal optionsNot all methods are available in all countries
RulesPlatforms have rules about taking clients off the platform, which can result in account problems
DisputesOutcomes depend on the platform's own processes
Account securityA suspended account can freeze your earnings

Do the maths

Before accepting a job, work out what you will receive after fees and conversions. Build those costs into your price.

Use the platform's tools properly

Use the platform's contracts, milestones and messaging so you are protected by its processes. Keep your communication and files on the platform, and do not move payment off-platform in ways that break the rules, since you will lose protection.

Keep a backup

Do not rely on a single platform for all your income. If an account is suspended, a backup channel keeps you afloat.

Efe's platform lesson

Efe calculates that, after fees and currency conversion, a $500 project will leave her roughly $420. She adjusts her price on the platform to reflect that, and uses milestones to protect larger jobs. She also continues to build her own clients through her portfolio and referrals. "The platform is a tool," she tells Ese. "Not my whole kitchen."

15Pricing So Fees And Costs Do Not Eat You

At the end of the year, Efe sits at her kitchen table with a calculator, a cup of tea and every invoice of the past twelve months. She wants to know the truth. When she finishes, she stares at the number for a long time, and then groans. "I earned less than I thought."

Let me show you how this happens, love, and how to prevent it.

The hidden costs of getting paid

CostWhat it is
Platform feesA percentage taken by marketplaces
Payment processing feesCharged by services for card or app payments
Transfer and conversion feesCharged for moving money across borders or currencies
Withdrawal feesCharged for moving money to your bank
Invoicing and accounting toolsSubscriptions
Software and assetsFonts, images, templates and tools for the project
Taxes and contributionsPayments you owe on your income
Unpaid timeTime spent finding clients, doing admin and revising beyond the scope

A worked example with illustrative numbers

ItemAmount
Project price$500
Platform fee (example 10 percent)-$50
Conversion and withdrawal costs (example)-$20
Software and image costs for the project-$25
Left before tax$405
Tax pot (example 25 percent of what remains)-$101
Left after tax pot$304
Hours spent on the project, including admin12
Real hourly rate after tax potAbout $25

This is an illustration, not a prediction. But look at what happened: a "$500 project" became about $25 an hour. If you thought you were earning $41 an hour, your plan could be badly off.

How to protect your price

  • Calculate your real take-home for each type of project.
  • Include costs in your price or list them as separate line items.
  • Set a minimum project fee.
  • State who pays transfer and platform fees in your agreement.
  • Track your hours, including admin and revisions.
  • Raise prices when your real hourly rate is lower than you want.

For a deeper look at pricing a business so it supports you, read how to build your first $3,000 a month online income system and the $1,000-to-$5,000 income ladder.

Efe's new minimums

Efe sets a minimum project fee, adds a small "tools and assets" line to her quotes and raises her price for new clients by 20 percent. Her inbox does not explode with complaints. Two prospects say no. Three say yes. By spring, her real hourly rate has risen noticeably. "Fewer clients, more money," she tells Ese. Ese says, "The best kind of maths."

16Your Thirty-Day Payment Setup Plan

On New Year's Eve, Efe takes her notebook to the balcony, with a cup of hot chocolate and a blanket, and writes a plan titled "How I Will Never Panic About Money Again." It is dramatic, and she knows it. But under it, she writes a list that is practical, and that I want to share with you, love.

Here is the plan, step by step. You can do it in thirty days, one small piece at a time.

Week one: Decide your terms

  • Day 1 to 2: Write your payment policy: deposit percentage, milestone structure for bigger projects, payment terms, late fee and kill fee.
  • Day 3 to 4: Decide your payment methods: one primary and one backup, and check fees and rules.
  • Day 5 to 7: Decide your minimum project fee and your policy for revisions and extras.

Week two: Build your documents

  • Day 8 to 10: Write your simple agreement template.
  • Day 11 to 12: Build your invoice template, with all the details.
  • Day 13 to 14: Write your reminder messages and your scripts for awkward conversations. Save them in one folder.

Week three: Build your money system

  • Day 15 to 16: Open a separate account or pot for business money.
  • Day 17 to 18: Set up your pots: tax, costs, buffer and your pay.
  • Day 19 to 20: Build your tracking sheet for invoices and payments.
  • Day 21: Read your government's guidance for self-employed people, and write your questions for an accountant.

Week four: Protect and practice

  • Day 22 to 23: Secure your accounts with strong passwords and two-step verification.
  • Day 24 to 25: Write your scam-safety rules, and review how to verify new clients.
  • Day 26 to 27: Practice your scripts out loud: the deposit request, the price increase and the late-payment reminder.
  • Day 28 to 29: Review your current clients: who has a clear agreement and deposit? Who needs one?
  • Day 30: Review your whole system. What is missing? What will you improve next month?

Where to find help

  • Your bank's website for payment options and international transfers.
  • Official government websites for tax and registration guidance.
  • Freelancer communities in your country, to learn what others use and which clients to be careful with.
  • A qualified accountant or adviser for tax and legal questions.
  • Professional bodies for your trade, which sometimes offer contract templates and guidance. Always check any template suits your country and project.

What to track after setup

NumberWhy
Invoices sent and paidYour payment rhythm
Average days to paymentYour cash-flow health
Overdue invoicesWhere to follow up
Real take-home per projectWhether your prices work
Buffer in monthsYour safety

Efe's thirty days

Efe follows the plan, a little each evening. By the end of the month, she has an agreement template, an invoice template, a reminder folder, a set of pots and a nervous but growing confidence. The next client who contacts her gets the full process: agreement, deposit, clear invoice. The client pays on time and says, "This was so organized." Efe says, "I am a person who is organized now." Ese says, "Do not let it go to your head."

17Common Mistakes (And How To Dodge Them)

Love, here are the mistakes I most want to save you from.

  • Working without a deposit. Take part of the payment upfront.
  • No written agreement. Put scope, revisions and payment in writing.
  • Invoicing late. Send the invoice the moment the work is delivered.
  • Vague due dates. State the date clearly.
  • Releasing all files before payment. Deliver final files after full payment, or in stages.
  • Ignoring fees and exchange rates. Know what actually lands.
  • Sending money back from an overpayment. This is a classic scam.
  • Relying on screenshots. Check your own account.
  • No buffer. One late payment should not be a crisis.
  • Mixing business and personal money. Separate them.
  • Avoiding taxes. Be curious and organized.
  • Apologizing for your price or terms. State them calmly.
  • Taking every client. Some clients are not worth it.
  • Never following up. A polite reminder sequence solves most late payments.

18When Things Do Not Go To Plan

Babe, here are some bumps you may meet, with ideas for getting through. Change one thing at a time.

What is happeningWhat it usually meansWhat to try
A client has not paid and is silentForgetfulness, approval delays or avoidanceFollow your reminder sequence; try a different channel; pause further work
A client disputes the work after deliveryUnclear scope or expectationsRefer to the agreement; offer a fair fix; keep records
Payment is much less than I expectedFees, conversion or unclear termsCheck each fee; adjust your price; state who pays fees
My income is lumpy and stressfulNo buffer or pay systemBuild pots, a buffer and a regular "salary"
A client wants to pay by an unusual methodPossible scam or inconvenienceVerify the client; use trusted methods; never send money back
A client wants me to start before signingPressure or disorganizationPolitely insist on a short agreement and deposit
I feel awkward asking for moneyNormal and commonUse scripts; practice aloud; remember payment is part of the job
A big client's payment is very slowLong terms and approvalsNegotiate terms in advance; build the delay into your cash flow

19Mindset: The Voices Around Money

Let me sit with you one last time, love, and talk about the voices in your head. Efe heard every one.

"I do not want to seem pushy"

Asking to be paid for work you completed is not pushy. It is professional. A clear policy applied to everyone is fair and kind.

"What if they get angry?"

Some might. A client who gets angry about a reasonable, agreed payment term is telling you something important about whether they are right for you.

"I should be grateful for any work"

You can be grateful and be paid fairly. Your skill, time and care have value, and gratitude is not a reason to work for free.

"I am bad with money"

Nobody is born good with money. It is a set of habits: deposits, invoices, pots, records. You can learn each one, a little at a time.

"What if I lose a client by asking?"

You might lose a client who would never have paid properly. Keep your pipeline full so no single client has too much power.

"It feels cold to be so organized about money"

Being organized is a way of caring: for your clients, because they know what to expect, and for yourself, because you can keep doing the work you love.

Hot Girl Reminder 💅 You do not have to be tough. You have to be clear, calm and consistent, and remember that payment is part of the work.
A good freelancer is not the one who never has late payers. It is the one who knows exactly what to do when they appear.

20Questions Girls Ask Me

How much deposit should I ask for?

Many freelancers ask for around half on small projects and use milestones for larger ones, but it depends on your field, the project and your client. Choose a policy and apply it consistently.

Do I need a contract for small jobs?

You need something in writing. Even a clear email covering scope, price, deadline, revisions and payment terms, which the client confirms, is much better than nothing. For larger projects, use a fuller agreement and consider professional advice.

What should I do if a client does not pay?

Follow a calm sequence: a friendly reminder, a firmer follow-up, a pause on work and a formal notice. Keep records, and consider further options, which depend on your country and the amount. Check local rules and, if the amount is significant, consider professional advice.

Can I charge a late fee?

Often yes, if it is agreed in writing in advance, and rules about late fees vary by country, so check what applies to you.

What is the best way to get paid from clients abroad?

It depends on your country and your clients' countries. Compare bank transfers, international payment services and platform payments for fees, speed, protection and availability, and check which are allowed and reliable where you live.

Should I invoice in my own currency or theirs?

It depends on practicality and risk. Many freelancers invoice in a widely used, more stable currency, and state who pays transfer fees. Always check what actually lands in your account.

What is an overpayment scam, and what do I do?

Someone sends you more than agreed and asks you to send back the difference. The original payment later turns out to be fake or reversed. Never send money back unless your bank confirms the original funds are final, and be very cautious.

Do I need to pay tax on freelance income?

In most places, yes, though rules vary. Check your government's official guidance, set aside a share of each payment and consider a qualified accountant.

How do I handle a client who wants a refund?

Check your agreement, stay calm and understand the problem. Offer a fair fix, partial refund or full refund depending on the situation and your policy.

How do I stop clients asking for extra work for free?

Define the scope and revisions in writing, and respond to extra requests with a friendly quote.

Should I work through freelance platforms?

They can help you find clients and provide payment protection, but they charge fees and have rules. Many freelancers use them alongside direct clients, and calculate their real take-home.

What if I cannot afford to lose a payment?

Take deposits, use milestones, keep a buffer, vet clients and avoid putting all your income in one client.

22One Last Thing, Love

You have read a very long guide, and that tells me you are serious about building something that lasts. Efe started with an unpaid invoice and a very long, unsent message. You are already further along than she was.

So here is what I want you to carry with you, the way I would say it with both your hands in mine. Getting paid is not a favour you ask for. It is the normal, expected end of doing good work, and it becomes calm when you set it up properly: a deposit, a clear agreement, a prompt invoice, a polite reminder sequence and a small cushion of savings. Most of the fear is in the vagueness. When you replace vagueness with a system, the fear shrinks.

Tonight, write your payment policy in six lines. Tomorrow, build your invoice template. By the end of the week, write your agreement and your reminder messages, and practice one awkward conversation out loud. Keep it small, keep it steady, and keep going when it is quiet.

I am rooting for you, babe. Do the work beautifully, and be paid for it, on time.
